reading.title: One Root, Many Directions
reading.purpose: Learn how the Latin root ced or cess and a prefix show which way things move.
paras: Look at the words precede, proceed, recede, secede, and intercede. They end the same way, and that is no accident. Each comes from the Latin verb cedere, which means "to go" or "to yield." The spelling cess, as in recession and procedure, is the same root in a different shape. Once you know the root, the first part of each word tells you which way things are going.

Pre- means "before," so to precede is to come before something. In a parade, the drum line precedes the floats. Pro- means "forward," so to proceed is to go forward, usually after a pause, as when a referee waves play on. Re- means "back," so water or fear can recede, moving away until it is smaller or gone. Se- means "apart," so to secede is to withdraw formally from a group. Inter- means "between," so a person who intercedes steps in between two sides to help.

The noun forms follow the same pattern. A recession is a time when business slows and many people lose jobs, so the economy seems to step backward. In the United States, the recession that began in December 2007 lasted until June 2009, about eighteen months. A procedure is a set of steps taken in order, such as the way a lab team cleans its tools. Successive events follow one another with no break, like five rainy days in a row.

Two more words show how the root reaches into everyday life. Something accessible is easy to reach or use, like a building with a ramp as well as stairs. Something excessive goes beyond what is reasonable, such as a recipe that calls for a full cup of salt. The prefix ex- means "out," so excessive means "going out past the limit." The next time a long word stops you, look for ced or cess. The direction is often the clue.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "recede" most nearly means
choices: to go ahead of something else
to move back until it is smaller or gone
to stop all movement at once
to step in between two sides in a disagreement
qs.why: The text says re- means "back," and it adds that water or fear can recede, "moving away until it is smaller or gone."

qs.q: Which sentence gives the dates of a real recession?
choices: A recession is a time when business slows and many people lose jobs, so the economy seems to step backward.
A procedure is a set of steps taken in order, such as the way a lab team cleans its tools.
Successive events follow one another with no break, like five rainy days in a row.
In the United States, the recession that began in December 2007 lasted until June 2009, about eighteen months.
qs.why: Only this sentence gives a start and an end for a recession: December 2007 to June 2009.

ev.text: In the United States, the recession that began in December 2007 lasted until June 2009, about eighteen months.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Latin roots matter only for the specialized words that scientists, doctors, and economists use.
Words that share a spelling at the end of the word always mean exactly the same thing.
A root plus a prefix can show the direction of movement in many English words.
The prefix ex- is the single most important part of any word that is built on a root.
qs.why: Each paragraph shows a prefix steering the same root in a new direction, and the last one tells readers to look for ced or cess.

qs.q: A library adds a ramp and an automatic door so that everyone can get inside. Which word from the reading describes the building now?
qs.why: The reading says something accessible is easy to reach or use, like a building with a ramp as well as stairs.
